rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 3.1-3.4 - own modelling chain (5 GCM-RCMs, 2 RCPs, Tetis hydrological model with 12 parameterizations, 2 irrigation scenarios) producing 240 simulations. Q2: Section 3.2.3 - model calibrated/evaluated against observed ETa, groundwater levels in four wells and plot-scale soil moisture of the study area; Section 4.1 and Figure 3 - simulations predict less recharge for drip than for flood irrigation; Section 4.3.2 - mean monthly recharge in control period 14.3 mm under drip vs 19.1 mm under flood; Section 4.4 - annual recharge 233-248 mm flood vs 169-175 mm drip; Conclusion 2 - recharge is higher in flood than in drip irrigation. Q4: Sections 2 and 3.2.1-3.2.3 - the model uses field-observed irrigation volumes (about 630 mm/yr flood vs 490 mm/yr drip), the observed drip wetting fraction (53%) and rooting depths, and simulates soil water storage (evaluated against observed soil moisture) from which recharge drains; Figure 4 - regime curves of irrigation volumes, ETa and R by month. Q6: Section 2 and Figure 1 - study area 913 km2 with 68 irrigation sectors (419 km2 irrigated); Section 3.2.1 - results aggregated at irrigation-sector scale; Section 4.4 - region-wide recharge effects of the planned transformation. Q8: Section 5.3 - farmer behaviour (cropping, pumping) not considered; constant irrigation schedules assumed; no CO2/vegetation feedback; static FAO crop-coefficient vegetation; Section 5.2 - climate-model uncertainty dominant. Q9: Figures 3-4 - shaded bands give the range of the five climate models around the median; Figures 5-7 - boxplots of 60 values (12 parameterizations x 5 climate models); Section 5.2 - drip/flood differences larger than climate prediction uncertainty.
rows.notes: Evidence is a calibrated distributed hydrological model, not direct measurement of recharge; the drip-vs-flood difference is a simulation outcome driven by the lower irrigation volumes and smaller wetted fraction under drip. Single modelling chain, so no triangulation. Q7 answered no because the reduced irrigation volume under drip and the business-as-usual schedule are described as inputs/assumptions rather than stated as requirements for the recharge effect. The passage's mechanism (return flows sustaining higher groundwater levels) is not explicitly tested; only recharge is simulated.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 3.1-3.4 - own modelling chain and 240 hydrological simulations for control, near-term and mid-term periods. Q2: Section 3.2.3 - model calibrated against observed ETa, groundwater and soil moisture in the study area; Section 4.3.1.1 and Figure 5 - significant recharge reductions only under RCP 8.5, more pronounced in drip than flood, from -2.4%/-6.6% (near term) to -7.3%/-9.3% (mid term); Section 4.4 and Figure 9 - planned expansion of drip further enhances the decreasing recharge trend (-5.1 to -7.0 mm/yr), with 100% drip reducing annual R by 31-35 mm; Conclusion 1 - decreasing mean recharge up to -6.6% flood and -9.3% drip. Q4: Sections 4.3.1.1 and Figure 4-5 - precipitation decrease (-6.5%/-6.6% mid term) and ETa changes are simulated alongside recharge; trends in mean R follow those in precipitation; Sections 3.2.1-3.2.3 - soil water storage, irrigation volumes and wetting fraction modelled. Q6: Section 2, Figure 1 - 913 km2 region, 68 irrigation sectors; Section 4.4 - regional water balance effects of transformation to 85% drip by 2030. Q7: Conclusion 1 and Key Points - the projected recharge and ETa changes hold under the assumption of a business-as-usual irrigation schedule; Section 4.3.1.1 - significant negative recharge changes only under RCP 8.5. Q8: Section 5.3 - farmer behaviour, future irrigation demand, CO2-vegetation feedbacks and dynamic vegetation not considered; Section 5.2 - uncertainty in magnitude and sign of change, climate models dominant. Q9: Figures 5-7 - boxplots of 60 values per case (12 parameterizations x 5 climate models) with circles for each climate model; Figures 3, 4 - ranges of the five climate models; Tables S1-S4 referenced for detail.
rows.notes: Supports the claim as a simulation-based projection; the drip-specific further reduction is a modelled outcome under fixed (business-as-usual) irrigation volumes, which the authors flag as a key assumption. 'Particularly under drier conditions' corresponds to RCP 8.5 and the mid-term future where precipitation declines. Single region (citrus, loam/clay-loam soils, semi-arid Mediterranean), single modelling approach.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Study is a regional hydrological modelling assessment (Tetis model, calibrated against observed ETa, groundwater levels and soil moisture) of flood vs drip irrigation under climate projections in Valencia, Spain. Q2 treated as yes because the model was evaluated against measurements from the real system, though future projections themselves cannot be validated.
